story: On February 23, 1987, a massive star in the Large Magellanic Cloud collapsed and exploded in a Type II supernova known as SN 1987A. Located roughly 168,000 light-years away, it was the closest observed supernova in over 400 years. Hours before visible light reached Earth, underground detectors registered a sudden burst of subatomic neutrinos, marking the first direct observation of supernova neutrinos and confirming core-collapse theories. Discovered by astronomers in Chile and New Zealand, the exploding star illuminated surrounding rings of circumstellar dust. For over three decades, the central compact object remained hidden behind dense dust clouds, sparking intense debates over whether it formed a black hole or a neutron star. Recently, observations from the ALMA radio array and the James Webb Space Telescope detected ionized argon emissions at the remnant center, providing definitive receipts that a superdense neutron star survived the cataclysmic blast.
angle: Ghostly subatomic neutrinos from SN 1987A blasted through Earth hours before any telescope saw the supernova light up the night sky.
